@Joachim Breitner Trying to understand exactly what lean-inductive-models is doing and guaranteeing, but the very long and very unwieldy readme did not help me a lot. Let me try something, and you (or others) can correct me.

Whenever you write an inductive declaration, lean-inductive-models generates an number of types/definitions/theorems, which model the inductive declaration, in the sense of the table in Output contract. This is almost exactly the same as the new constants that the kernel adds to the environment through the inductive declaration, except that in the kernel the equations are definitional equalities, while in lim these are theorems stated with propositional equality. (Is this correspondence between the types generated by the kernel and those inhabited by lim tested? or do we have to trust that?) All this is done using only the built-in types of Lean (dependent function types, universes), and the four "inductive-like" types listed in Idea:

Eq Nat PUnit PSigma' Quot

This is not a general claim of soundness of the whole class of inductive types (which would require a verified translation), but more in the style of translation validation. However, up to the difference between defeq and propeq, this provides an "on-the-fly" justification of inductive definitions. (And moreover that difference in equality is not critical for soundness, because the set-theoretic model is extensional anyway, ie it conflates defeq and propeq)

Yes. The even shorter summary: it is a translation validation of user defined inductives into an extensional type system with only few hardcoded inductives.

The difference to the in kernel reduction for nested inductives is that it proves iota/eta etc rules.

It's certainly not the endgame (verification is better than translation validation), but I believe it can help to have a first step: translate inductives, verify a checker over the result. And then iteratively let fewer indictives be translated and more of them accepted with a verified guard.
(and yes, the phasing in the post mortem oversells it. I signed that off too carelessly. I am really not good at reviewing, too trusting by character)

Yeah @Joachim Breitner I was very scared when I clicked on Leo's comment saying that the class of inductives Lean implements are "fully understood" and it led to this repository that was implemented by Claude and seemed to be certifying rather than certified.... and to certainly not correspond to any kind of understanding...

Not saying it's not useful, I think certifying approaches are super pragmatic, but seeing Leo tout this as some kind of proof that more type theory work isn't needed made me want to throw up from anxiety. (I doubt you'd agree with his comment tbh, and if I'm right, please do correct him on the blog post)

I do think the "defeq is not critical for soundness" sentence is questionable though @Meven Lennon-Bertrand , no? Because weird properties of def eq have somehow caused soundness bugs, like the recent one that took advantage of the fact that Lean's defeq is not actually transitive. And still I have a strong suspicion more lurk in primitive projections, even though "all they do" is expose some def eqs

I am putting together a one-pager for funders about supporting the type theory side of this, both for Lean and beyond that (including any potential later extensions of Lean that might touch the kernel!), but Leo's blog post made that job of mine a lot harder by essentially giving the impression that such work is not needed now that Joachim's repo exists.

Talia Ringer said:

I do think the "defeq is not critical for soundness" sentence is questionable though Meven Lennon-Bertrand , no?

Sorry, this was rather unclear of me. What I meant is that, on the type theory side, both for consistency and for the set theoretic model, the separation between defeq and propeq is not really relevant. The set theoretic model is extensional (conflates defeq and propeq), and it's an old result of Hofmann (refined by @Théo Winterhalter) that in the presence of UIP + funext in fact extensional type theory is conservative (proves the same theorems) as intentional type theory. Hence, while this difference between defeq and propeq is important from the pov of type checking and implementation, from the pov of type theoretic soundness/building a model, it is not really that important.

Yep, and the correction never travels as far…
Is lean-inductive-models available in Comparitor? Especially since it is the official safeguard against possible unsoundness of Lean’s inductives?
(I was thinking about this today when trying to convince the EpochAI Erdos eval to use Nanoda in Comparator.)

Since a short while, comparator can be instructed to use other kernels, so you can use lean-inductive-models with it.

But lean-inductive-models is not the official safeguard against possible unsoundness of Lean’s inductive. It is, at most, one additional safeguard, part of the story that multiple checkers help guard against implementation bugs. It is true that it caught most of the most recent bugs found, but it is no more or less relevant than the official kernel, lean4lean or nanoda in that way – and much less battle tested at that.

TBC, I’m not saying that we shouldn’t use Nanoda, etc but that we should use lean-inductive-models as one of the few canconical additional kernels. I would say if Palomar especially is not using it, that is a problem. (Same it was never used on the FLT proof.)

As for it if it is the only safeguard, what others are there (before the type theory work that the type theorists here are doing)? We don’t even have a pen and paper proof that Lean’s full inductive is consistent, right? (But at the same, it seems to be a pretty good safeguard to me. The two worst cases are that it is incomplete [but so what if it works in practice] and that it could change the propositional semantics [but that’s also is midigated by running with and without it]. Right?)
